non_mechanical_rationales.reason: Common terminology and sentence precision are partly judgment-based; tests cover activation and fixtures, while review applies the prose judgment.
Inline versus display formatting depends on readability and importance; tests cover policy activation and reviewers decide borderline cases.
Common graph-theoretic and TCS terminology is discipline-specific and sometimes context-sensitive; review applies the policy after mechanical activation checks.
The amount of informal lead-in before a result depends on the result's role and local context.
Section outlines are prose-level checks; deterministic tests verify the requirement is active, and review assesses the paragraph quality.
Whether a proof is long or important enough for an opening paragraph is a mathematical writing judgment.
Equation display decisions depend on length, alignment, and importance; mechanical checks can only flag candidates for review.
Command-style sentence openings can be partly scanned mechanically, but deciding whether a standard disciplinary opening is clearer requires prose review.
Abstract content depends on the contribution and venue; the checklist is mandatory to consider but not a fixed sentence order.
Removing headings and citation markers is a temporary readability test whose result requires prose judgment.
Whether a figure materially clarifies structure is a semantic judgment; figure production remains a separate routed workflow.
Whether a definition is standard for the intended audience depends on the verified source, concept, edition, and notation.
The balance among context, result, method, and technical detail depends on the item and intended database reader.
Exceptional reviews and historical books are examples for judgment, not service requirements or fixed templates.

Sentence boundaries in LaTeX source can be obscured by abbreviations, commands, comments, and environments, so automated checks can flag candidates but prose review confirms compliance; rendered PDF wrapping is outside the rule.

Whether deleting ordinary source content is genuinely necessary depends on the requested outcome; review must distinguish restorable content edits from whole-file management, while confidentiality, privacy, security, licensing, anonymization, redaction, and unsafe-content boundaries require removal.
The contribution thesis depends on the item, its literature context, and the intended database reader, and must remain factual rather than promotional.
The number and choice of representative results depend on the structure of the item and the explanatory role each result serves.
Whether a verified contribution supports an importance, novelty, or significance claim requires mathematical and literature judgment.

Determining whether context supplies an assumption, whether a proposed assumption merely rescues a claim, and whether an issue is a proof gap or false theorem requires exact-version mathematical review.
